chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Sa'id from Hammad ibn Isa from Hariz from Muhammad ibn Muslim from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him)

He was asked about the beasts of birds and wild animals, until hedgehogs, ostriches, donkeys, mules, and horses were mentioned to him. He said: 'The forbidden is only that which Allah has forbidden in His Book. And the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) forbade eating the meat of donkeys on the day of Khaybar, and he forbade them only because their numbers would be exhausted, and the donkeys are not forbidden.'

Say: 'I do not find in that which has been revealed to me to be forbidden to one who eats it, unless it be a dead animal, or blood poured out, or the flesh of swine, for indeed it is impure, or a transgression that was offered to other than Allah.'

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: His saying (peace be upon him) 'The forbidden is only that which Allah has forbidden in His Book' means that the specifically forbidden, strictly prohibited thing is only that which Allah has mentioned in the Quran. And although there are many other forbidden things, they are lesser in strictness. And that which indicates this is what has been narrated.
ai.seo_question: What is the difference between the permanently forbidden foods in the Quran and other temporarily forbidden foods like donkey meat?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) distinguishes between permanent, severe divine prohibitions (haram al-mukhassas) explicitly listed in the Quran and temporary or lesser prohibitions (haram al-mu'assal) derived from Prophetic practice, such as the ban on donkey meat at Khaybar due to military utility. This hadith establishes a key Shia jurisprudential principle that not all Prophetic dietary restrictions carry the same weight as Quranic mandates, allowing for flexibility in cases of necessity or changing circumstances.
